ex: How many carats is this diamond?
She wears a two-carat diamond ring.
This small stone weighs half a carat.
The price of a diamond depends on its carats.
carat.note: For gold, American English usually spells it "karat": 18-karat gold.

ex: She wore a gold medallion on a long chain.
Each winner got a silver medallion and a prize.
He bought a small medallion as a gift for his mom.
The medallion has a picture of a lion on it.
I use a desktop at work and a laptop at home.
Is a desktop cheaper than a good laptop?
Our office bought ten new desktops this year.
My old desktop is too slow for new games.
desktop.note: Also the main computer screen with icons: "Save the file to your desktop."

ex: My cousin is a real coffee snob.
Don't be a snob about cheap restaurants.
She became a bit of a snob after moving to the city.
Only a snob would laugh at his old car.

ping.note: Most often "ping" is a short high sound or a quick message: "Send me a ping."

henry.note: Most often "Henry" is a man's name. The unit is written with a small h: "two henries."

tariff.note: Usually a tax on goods from other countries. A phone price plan is a "plan," not a "tariff."

doctorate.note: The most common doctorate is a PhD: "She has a PhD in biology."

complex.note: Most often "complex" is an adjective meaning difficult: "a complex problem."

cholera.note: Uncountable: get cholera, a cholera outbreak (not "a cholera").

ex: Chi is the 22nd letter of the Greek alphabet.
The Greek letter chi looks like the letter X.
Our math teacher wrote chi on the board.
In statistics, we often use the chi-square test.
chi.note: Said like "kai." Most often "chi" means life energy in Chinese ideas, as in "tai chi."

salaam.note: A Muslim greeting that means "peace"; often in "salaam alaikum."

fudge.note: Uncountable: a piece of fudge (not "a fudge").

ex: Make a checklist before your trip.
The pilot went through the safety checklist.
I check off each item on my checklist.
Here is a checklist for your first day at work.

soul.note: Most often "soul" means the spirit of a person: "She has a kind soul."

phoenix.note: Most often "Phoenix" is a big US city in Arizona. The bird is written "phoenix."

nylon.note: Uncountable: made of nylon. "Nylons" (plural) are women's stockings.

exclusive.note: Most often "exclusive" is an adjective: "an exclusive club," "an exclusive interview."

paparazzi.note: Plural noun; one photographer is a "paparazzo."

ex: Soccer hooligans fought outside the stadium after the game.
The police arrested several hooligans last night.
A group of hooligans broke the bus windows.
Why are those hooligans shouting in the street?
The Sheikh ul-Islam was the top religious leader in the Ottoman Empire.
In the past, the sultan chose the Sheikh ul-Islam.
The Sheikh ul-Islam gave advice on questions of Islamic law.
Our guide showed us where the Sheikh ul-Islam once lived.
Sheikh ul-Islam.note: A title for a top Muslim religious leader, mostly in the Ottoman Empire.

ex: The new ad campaign starts next week.
Our team planned a social media campaign for the shop.
The campaign helped us sell more phones this year.
How much did the TV ad campaign cost?
campaign.note: Most often a "campaign" is a plan of actions to win an election or change something.

provider.note: Most often "provider" means any company or person giving a service: "a health care provider."

ex: The villain in the movie is a cold sociopath.
A sociopath often does not feel guilt.
She thought her old boss was a real sociopath.
Doctors say a sociopath can seem very charming.

alderman.note: In some US cities, a member of the city council.

Frau.note: A German word, used as a title for German women, like "Mrs."

silicone.note: Uncountable. Don't confuse with "silicon," the element used in computer chips.

piercing.note: Also an adjective: "a piercing scream" (very loud and high).
